1.1.given: A fact we are told to accept at the start of a problem.
1.1.measurement: A number found with a tool, like a ruler or protractor, with a unit.
1.1.assumption: Something we accept without checking. Good work says its assumptions out loud.
1.1.proof: A chain of reasons that shows a statement must be true.
1.1.not to scale: The drawing's sizes may be wrong, so use the labels, not your eyes.

1.2.inductive reasoning: Spotting a pattern in examples and guessing it always holds.
1.2.conjecture: A guess based on a pattern that has not been proved yet.
1.2.counterexample: One example that makes a statement false.
1.2.for every: Means the statement must work in all cases, not just most.

1.3.point: An exact location with no size. We describe it but do not define it.
1.3.line: A straight path of points that goes on forever both ways. Undefined, like point.
1.3.plane (undefined): A flat surface that goes on forever in every direction. Undefined, like point and line.
1.3.collinear: Points that all lie on one line.
1.3.coplanar: Points or lines that all lie in one plane.
1.3.segment: Part of a line between two endpoints, including the endpoints.
1.3.ray: Part of a line that starts at one point and goes on forever one way.
1.3.parallel lines: Lines in the same plane that never meet.

1.4.angle: Two rays that share an endpoint.
1.4.vertex: The shared endpoint of an angle's two rays.
1.4.ray: Part of a line that starts at one point and goes on forever one way.
1.4.central angle: An angle whose vertex is the center of a circle.
1.4.arc: A piece of a circle between two points on it.
1.4.chord: A segment whose endpoints are both on a circle.
1.4.model assumption: A simplifying idea we accept so a real situation fits the math.

1.5.polygon: A closed flat shape made of segments that meet only at their ends.
1.5.vertex: A corner of a polygon, where two sides meet.
1.5.side: One of the segments that make up a polygon.
1.5.diagonal: A segment joining two corners of a polygon that are not next to each other.
1.5.convex: No dents: every diagonal stays inside the shape.
1.5.regular: All sides equal and all angles equal.
1.5.polyhedron: A solid whose faces are all polygons.

1.6.construction: A drawing made with only a compass and a straightedge.
1.6.compass: A tool for drawing circles and copying lengths.
1.6.straightedge: A ruler with no marks, used only to draw straight lines.
1.6.circle: All the points in a plane the same distance from one center point.
1.6.center: The fixed point every point of the circle is the same distance from.
1.6.radius: The distance from the center to the circle, or a segment with that length.
1.6.arc: A piece of a circle between two points on it.

1.7.undefined term: A basic word we describe but do not define, like point, line and plane.
1.7.definition: An exact meaning built from words we already have.
1.7.postulate (axiom): A starting rule we accept without proof.
1.7.theorem: A statement that has been proved from definitions, postulates and earlier theorems.

1.8.converse: Swap the if and then parts.
1.8.contrapositive: Swap the parts and add 'not' to both. It is true exactly when the original is.
1.8.truth table: A chart that lists every true/false case for a statement.

1.9.biconditional ('if and only if'): A statement where the conditional and its converse are both true.
1.9.definition: An exact meaning. Every good definition works as an 'if and only if' statement.
1.9.example: A case that fits the definition.
1.9.non-example: A case that does not fit the definition, which helps show its edges.
1.9.counterexample: One example that makes a statement false.

1.10.given: A fact we are told to accept at the start of a proof.
1.10.prove: The statement the proof must reach.
1.10.definition: An exact meaning we can use as a reason in a proof.
1.10.property: A rule that numbers or shapes always follow, used as a reason.
1.10.integers add to integers: Adding two whole numbers (positive, negative or zero) always gives another one.

1.11.indirect proof: A proof that assumes the opposite of what we want and shows that leads to something impossible.
1.11.contradiction: Two statements that cannot both be true.
1.11.at least one: One or more. Its opposite is 'none'.
1.11.none: Not even one. Its opposite is 'at least one'.

1.12.deductive system: A body of math built from starting terms and rules using only logic.
1.12.undefined (starting) term: A basic word we describe but do not define.
1.12.definition: An exact meaning built from words we already have.
1.12.postulate: A starting rule we accept without proof.
1.12.rule of inference: An allowed logical step from statements we have to a new one.
1.12.theorem: A statement proved inside the system.
1.12.conjecture: A guess that has not been proved yet.
1.12.not proved yet: We do not know whether it is true or false, so we cannot use it as a reason.
